intro: Couperin places an Italian-style trio sonata before the French dances of La Piémontaise, played here by four musicians sharing three written parts. How do the two upper lines exchange the lead above their shared bass?
question: How do three musical lines become a conversation?

relations.label: The first air returns
relations.basis: Inside the paired airs, the opening major-mode material returns after the minor-mode contrast. This agrees with the air at 274 s and the return to major described by the listening note near 450 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.966, sustained 37 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 158 s (cache/form/couperin-nations-piemontaise.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Three parts, four players
cues.text: Violin and flute carry the two upper parts; viol and keyboard share the bass. Through the opening, listen for the relationship between those lines: one can sustain a note while another moves, making harmony out of their overlap.
cues.evidence: The score has two upper parts and a bass; Commons identifies the four players in this recording.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An estimated lower pitch
cues.text: This recording appears to use a pitch near A = 415 Hz, about a semitone below modern A = 440. That is an estimate, not a documented tuning choice; the score’s G minor would therefore sound lower than on a modern piano.
cues.evidence: The recording’s estimated pitches repeatedly fall about a semitone below the written music; the performers do not document a pitch standard.

cues.title: An inherited organ loft
cues.text: Couperin’s father Charles was organist of Saint-Gervais in Paris. After Charles died in 1679, the post was reserved for the young François; Lalande held it until he could take over.
cues.evidence: The Opéra Royal de Versailles biography describes Charles’s death, François’s succession and Lalande’s interim service.

cues.title: Quicker exchanges
cues.text: The first quick section gives the upper lines shorter figures to exchange. Follow the changing relationship between the parts rather than assigning one a permanent melody role and the other a permanent accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The first Vivement follows the slow opening in the score; increased activity around 1:30 supports approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Alternating kinds of pace
cues.text: The sonade alternates quick sections with more sustained ones. Around this transition, compare how much space the longer notes leave between gestures, rather than expecting one dance rhythm to continue throughout.
cues.evidence: The score places a Gravement after the first Vivement; reduced activity around 2:10–2:35 supports the broad transition.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An Italian disguise
cues.text: In the preface to Les Nations, Couperin says he first presented a sonata as the work of an Italian whose name was an anagram of his own. Its success encouraged him to write more. This is Couperin’s account, not an independently witnessed episode.
cues.evidence: Brian Robins’s Early Music Review article recounts the story from Couperin’s preface.

cues.title: Quick and marked
cues.text: The next quick section is marked “Vivement et marqué”. Listen for how distinct beginnings help separate the upper lines’ short figures above the bass; articulation can clarify imitation without changing the ensemble.
cues.evidence: The score gives this marking; renewed activity after the low-level interval around 3:20 supports approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A royal chapel organist
cues.text: In 1693 Couperin became an organist of Louis XIV’s royal chapel. His publications include organ masses, sacred vocal music, harpsichord pieces and chamber music: the same musician worked across church and court settings.
cues.evidence: The Opéra Royal de Versailles biography records the 1693 appointment and these categories of work.

cues.title: The graceful airs
cues.text: The central airs ask for a more graceful manner than the preceding quick exchanges. Follow the shape of a whole melodic phrase across its smaller ornaments, keeping the bass line in view.
cues.evidence: The score labels the airs “gracieusement”; a low-level interval around 4:30 and less frequent attacks afterwards support their approximate location.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ornament and main note
cues.text: Throughout the airs, distinguish principal notes from the ornaments around them. Listen for how a trill or a brief turn shapes the approach to a resting point, rather than counting each small note as a new melodic destination.
cues.evidence: This is a guide to ornamented melodic lines, not an identification of a particular trill in the recording.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Four names in print
cues.text: Les Nations appeared in 1726 as four ordres: La Françoise, L’Espagnole, L’Impériale and La Piémontaise. Each joins an Italian-style sonata to a sequence of French dances.
cues.evidence: The publication’s titles and date are listed by Opéra Royal de Versailles; Brian Robins describes the sonata-and-suite design.

cues.title: A keyboard teaching book
cues.text: Couperin published L’Art de toucher le clavecin in 1716, between his first and second books of harpsichord pieces. His work as a teacher accompanied his performing and composing posts.
cues.evidence: The Opéra Royal de Versailles biography records the treatise’s 1716 publication and Couperin’s harpsichord teaching.

cues.title: Corelli beside Lully
cues.text: Couperin’s preface names both Corelli and Lully as composers he admired. The combination of an Italian-style sonata with French dances makes that double allegiance part of the collection’s design.
cues.evidence: Brian Robins quotes the preface’s acknowledgement of Corelli and Lully in Early Music Review.

cues.title: A measured closing section
cues.text: The later slow section is marked “Gravement et marqué”, before the final quick passage. Compare its deliberate articulation with the airs: the same small ensemble can distinguish sections through pace and phrasing rather than a change of instruments.
cues.evidence: The score’s movement order supplies the contrast; a low-level interval near 8:30 supports this approximate location.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last quick exchange
cues.text: The concluding “Légèrement” restores quicker movement. Follow the bass beneath the upper lines so that their short figures do not obscure the direction of each phrase.
cues.evidence: The score ends the sonade with Légèrement; more frequent attacks from roughly 9:05 support the passage’s placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sonade’s final cadence
cues.text: The closing passage brings the sonade to a cadence. In the complete La Piémontaise, an allemande follows to begin the French dance sequence; this recording stops before those dances.
cues.evidence: The score’s movement list places the allemande next; the recording analysis shows the sonade fading to near silence by 10:00.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Long overlaps become short exchanges
transitions.how: The opening’s sustained upper lines give way to the shorter, quicker figures of Vivement. Violin and flute remain equal participants: the change is from overlapping long notes to more frequent exchanges, not from an introduction to a solo with accompaniment. G minor remains the home-key reference, while viol and keyboard keep the common bass audible beneath the busier counterpoint. Couperin makes the seam through pace and articulation, without needing a new instrumental colour.
transitions.evidence: The 1:30 section boundary agrees with increasing attack density, from about two attacks per second near 1:25 to 4.2 near 1:35. The published movement order and existing score-based cue identify Gravement followed by Vivement and the shorter upper-part exchanges. Written G minor is distinguished from the recording’s approximately semitone-lower pitch; no individual cadence is inferred from the analysis.

transitions.title: The quick conversation makes room for held notes
transitions.how: The first Vivement gives way to another Gravement rather than extending its quick figures into a continuous dance. Longer upper notes make their overlap with the changing bass more exposed: listen for tension between a note still held and the harmony newly arriving below it. The violin and flute retain their separate lines, with viol and keyboard supplying the same shared bass. The ensemble has not changed; the amount of time available to hear each vertical combination has.
transitions.evidence: The 2:14 section boundary is an analysis change within the strong 2:08–2:22 cluster, following a low-level window near 2:10. The score’s Vivement–Gravement succession and sustained trio texture supply the description. The span is deliberately broad; no particular suspension or modulation chord has been aligned.

transitions.title: The marked figures yield to an air
transitions.how: After the distinctly attacked figures of Vivement et marqué, the first air asks for gracieusement: the ear follows a longer melodic phrase through its ornaments. Its G-major colour replaces the sonade’s home-key B♭ with B♮. The continuo still supplies the bass beneath two upper lines, but their graceful phrasing matters more than the preceding passage’s quick exchanges. This first air will return after the minor-key air; the major colour introduced here therefore becomes something recognisable later.
transitions.evidence: The 4:34 section boundary follows a strong change and near-silence at 4:30, with fewer attacks after the restart. The score labels the airs gracieusement; the form relation identifies the major first air at 4:34.5–5:11.5 and its return at 7:12.5–7:49.5 after the minor air. Keys are written pitches, not the lower sounding estimates. The exact cadential chord before the air is not claimed.

transitions.title: Measured weight gives way to light motion
transitions.how: The final Gravement et marqué is a short weighty preparation, not the sonade’s ending. Légèrement releases it into quicker movement, with the two treble parts again exchanging figures over the continuo bass. The conclusion brings the music back through G-minor territory towards the sonade’s final cadence; this is not yet the allemande that begins the following French suite. Listen to the bass’s phrase endings beneath the light upper activity: they give the conclusion its punctuation.
transitions.evidence: The 9:05 section boundary agrees with attack density rising to about 4.6 per second from 1.4 near 9:00. The published order gives Gravement et marqué followed by Légèrement, then an allemande outside this recording; the late pitch estimates are compatible with written G minor at the inferred lower tuning. No exact closing chord or literal return of an earlier theme is asserted.

facts: Nephew of Louis Couperin; succeeded his father Charles at Saint-Gervais
Organist of Saint-Gervais from 1685; royal chapel organist from 1693; royal chamber harpsichordist from 1717
Four books of harpsichord pieces, 27 ordres; organ masses, chamber music, motets and Leçons de Ténèbres
composer.background:
François Couperin belonged to a family whose connection with the organ of Saint-Gervais in Paris lasted for generations. His father Charles died in 1679, when François was ten; Michel-Richard de Lalande temporarily held the post intended for the boy. Couperin took it up in 1685. His uncle Louis, who had died before François was born, had already established a distinctive harpsichord language of broken chords, dance rhythms and unmeasured preludes. The younger Couperin inherited a profession and a repertory. His own published harpsichord music would increasingly substitute named character pieces for a predictable succession of dances.

In 1693 he won one of the four organist positions at Louis XIV’s royal chapel. Serving by quarter, he combined court employment with his Parisian responsibilities. He taught members of the royal family and took part in chamber performances; in 1717 he became a royal chamber harpsichordist. These overlapping appointments help explain his range: a musician who supplied an organ verset for a service might also teach the fingering of an ornament or play a concert with violin and viol.
composer.epithet: A Parisian organist whose harpsichord pieces turn ornament, delayed resolution and the timing of a released key into structural events.
